text: It's the sixteenth of September, nineteen-oh-eight. And a man from Flint is about to create a car company that will become the biggest in the world.
subs: It's 16 September 1908.
And a man from Flint is about to create a car company

text: His name is William Crapo Durant. Everyone calls him Billy. He isn't an engineer. He's a salesman.

text: Twenty-two years earlier, in eighteen eighty-six, he borrowed fifteen hundred dollars and bought the rights to a two-wheeled road cart. With a partner, Dallas Dort, he started building them in Flint.
subs: Twenty-two years earlier, in 1886,
he borrowed $1,500 and bought the
rights to a two-wheeled road cart.

text: By nineteen hundred, the Durant-Dort Carriage Company was the biggest carriage maker in America. Flint put up an arch over its main street. Vehicle City.
subs: By 1900, the Durant-Dort Carriage Company

Flint put up an arch over its main street: Vehicle City.

text: Then the vehicles changed. In nineteen-oh-four, Durant took over a small, struggling company called Buick. He sold Buicks the way he had sold carts, and Buick grew faster than anyone could build them.

text: And the people came. In nineteen hundred, Flint had thirteen thousand people. By nineteen thirty, it had more than a hundred and fifty thousand.

By 1930, it had more than 150,000.

text: This is what working there looked like, filmed inside Chevrolet's Flint plants in nineteen thirty-six. The foundry. The presses. The line. Fast, hot, and never stopping.

text: The pay was better than on any farm. But the men on the line had no say over how fast it ran, or who was laid off when it slowed.

text: The union has a plan. General Motors makes almost all its car bodies from steel dies, the giant moulds that stamp out the panels. And there are only two sets. One in Cleveland. One here, in Fisher Body Plant Number One.
